extracted.intended_audience: journalism educators, communication researchers, high-school publication advisers
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, administering, and interpreting a questionnaire study profiling college newswriting students on career choice, media use, and perceptions of media credibility, comparing those with and without high-school publication experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: High school publication experience (staffer vs nonstaffer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the student 'had worked on high school publications' (former staffers) or had not (nonstaffers) — used as the principal grouping variable for comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare former staffers with nonstaffers on career interests, timing of career decision, media credibility ratings, and media use. The paper reports subgroup percentages and t-tests/chi-square tests to assess differences (e.g., staffers decided earlier to enter communications; staffers used more media).

rubrics_metrics.name: Most-enjoyed high school publication activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey item asking what former staffers enjoyed most about high school publications (options include writing, layout, photography, interviewing, editing, reporting, business).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use frequencies/percentages to rank activities; findings here: writing and layout were top choices (writing most often, layout a close second), with photography and interviewing next and editing/reporting/business less often mentioned. Implication: advisers should recognize layout as a strong motivator as well as writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest in different media careers (job preference ranking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students indicate interest in various careers (magazines, newspapers, broadcasting, public relations, advertising, photography, communication research, teaching).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare distributions between staffers and nonstaffers using t-tests or chi-square. Results: staffers more likely to prefer magazines and newspapers; nonstaffers more likely to prefer advertising. Also report sex differences (males vs females) and institutional program-structure effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of decision to pursue communication career
rubrics_metrics.description: When the student first decided to go into communication — by grade level (before 9th, 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th, in college) or 'haven't decided.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-tabulations to compare staffers and nonstaffers; staffers tended to decide earlier (many during high school and a substantial portion before 12th grade). Statistical significance reported (e.g., p=.000 for differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception/ranking of media credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If hearing conflicting reports of the same news story from five sources, which source would you be most inclined to believe? (options: television, newspaper, magazine, radio, other people).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report percentages by subgroup and test differences. Findings: Alabama students overall rated television highest; Indiana students rated television and newspapers close. Staffers tended to choose newspapers/magazines more than nonstaffers, who favored television/radio. State differences may affect significance (chi-square values and p reported).

rubrics_metrics.name: Most important source of impressions about communication careers
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey item asking what was the most important source of impressions about communication careers (radio & TV, family & friends, media professionals, newspapers & magazines, high school adviser, movies, books).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabulate and compare staffers vs nonstaffers and by institution. Guidance: staffers were more likely than nonstaffers to cite a high school adviser; institutional patterns differ (e.g., Alabama: radio/TV and media pros prominent; Indiana: newspapers/magazines and media pros). Report significance where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media use intensity and habits (newspapers, magazines, broadcast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of media consumption: frequency of reading specific newspapers (campus daily, local paper, metropolitan papers), regular reading of newsmagazines (Newsweek, Time, U.S. News), attention to broadcast news (network newscast 'last night', local newscast, programs like '60 Minutes' and 'Lou Grant'), and estimated time spent daily with newspapers, radio, and television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute proportions who read each outlet 'regularly' and average time categories (e.g., 20+ minutes/day for newspapers, 1–2 hours/day TV). Compare subgroups: staffers used more media (p=.047); Alabama students heavier users of electronic media than Indiana (significant p-values reported). Use these measures to estimate total weekly media hours per student.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type/level of responsibility in high school publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether former staffers held responsible positions on publications (editor or section editor) and whether they received academic credit for publications experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report percentages (e.g., more than half were editors/section editors; ~60% received academic credit). Use this to identify high-quality recruits: students in responsible positions are more likely to be interested in journalism careers and are recommended recruitment targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument design: questionnaire items and administration timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a refined questionnaire given in the first month of the semester to all students enrolled in the basic newswriting course; items cover background, high-school publication experience, career interests, timing of decision, source of career information, media credibility ranking, and media use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure most items identical across sites with minor tailoring for institutional differences; administer at course start to profile incoming students. Use t-tests and chi-square analyses to compare groups and report p-values for significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruiting target and timing recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations for university recruiting: focus on students who are editors and section editors of high-school publications; recruit earlier than senior year (inform in 8th–10th grades and then focus on responsible juniors and seniors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities desiring to recruit top quality students should identify and engage high-responsibility scholastic publication students and work with high-school advisers as an important resource for career and enrollment guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational/teaching obligation for critical media use
rubrics_metrics.description: Both high school teachers and college instructors have an obligation to help students learn to use media wisely by encouraging reading daily newspapers, comparing accounts across outlets, and continually asking questions about media credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement classroom activities that connect students' heavy media exposure with classroom/library study—encourage comparing the same incident across daily newspapers, newsmagazines, and broadcasts to develop astute media consumers and better communicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistical tests and reporting (significance, p-values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of t-tests and chi-square tests to compare staffers and nonstaffers on career interests, timing of decision, credibility ratings, and media use, with reporting of chi-square values, degrees of freedom, and p-values (e.g., X^2=13.88, 4 df, p=.0077).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating subgroup differences, report the test statistic, degrees of freedom, and p-value. Note institutional differences may affect statistical significance; interpret results accordingly rather than overgeneralizing.
